topicTitle: Structured Data: Objects, JSON & The URL API

lessons.title: Object Literals & Key-Value Pair Operations
lessons.description: Objects store data as key-value pairs — they're the most common way to group related information in JavaScript.

sections.heading: What is an object?
paragraphs: An object is a collection of properties, where each property has a key (name) and a value. Think of it like a real-world object — a car has a color, a brand, and a speed. In code, those become key-value pairs.
list: Keys are always strings (or symbols)
Values can be any data type: strings, numbers, booleans, arrays, functions, or even other objects
Objects are created with curly braces {}

sections.heading: Creating objects
paragraphs: You create an object using literal syntax — just curly braces with key-value pairs separated by commas. Each key is followed by a colon and its value.
list: Use colons : to separate key from value
Separate properties with commas ,
Keys with spaces or special characters need quotes: {"my key": value}

codeExamples.heading: Creating a basic object
explanation: Each property is a key-value pair: name: "Alex".
Access values using dot notation: person.name.
Objects can mix different value types — strings, numbers, and booleans in one object.

codeExamples.heading: Adding and updating properties
explanation: Add properties by assigning to a new key: car.color = "blue".
Update by reassigning to an existing key: car.year = 2022.
Remove with delete: delete car.color.

practice.task: Create an object called book with properties: title, author, pages, and isRead. Then add a new property called genre and change pages to a different number.
hints: Start with let book = { title: "...", author: "...", pages: 200, isRead: false };
practice.note: Objects are mutable — you can add, change, and remove properties at any time.

keyTakeaways: Objects store data as key-value pairs using curly braces {}.
Access values with dot notation (obj.key) or bracket notation (obj["key"]).
You can add, update, and delete properties dynamically.
lessons.challenge: Create an object for a recipe with name, ingredients (an array), cookTime, and servings. Add a new property called difficulty with a value of "easy".

lessons.title: Dot Notation vs Dynamic Bracket Notation Access
lessons.description: Two ways to access object properties — dot notation for known keys, bracket notation for dynamic keys.

sections.heading: Dot notation
paragraphs: Dot notation is the simplest way to access properties — just put a dot after the object name and the key. It's clean and easy to read when you know the exact property name.
list: Use when the property name is known and simple
Syntax: object.propertyName
Cannot use with dynamic keys or keys with spaces

sections.heading: Bracket notation
paragraphs: Bracket notation uses square brackets and a string. It's more powerful because you can use variables, computed expressions, or keys with special characters.
list: Use when the key is stored in a variable
Syntax: object["propertyName"] or object[variableName]
Required for keys with spaces, hyphens, or special characters

codeExamples.heading: Dot vs bracket notation
explanation: Dot notation is cleaner for known, simple keys like firstName.
Bracket notation is required for keys with spaces like "last name".
Bracket notation with a variable lets you access properties dynamically — the key is determined at runtime.

codeExamples.heading: Dynamic property access
explanation: When you use a variable in brackets, JavaScript looks up its value and uses that as the key.
You can build key names dynamically: "font" + "Size" becomes "fontSize".
Bracket notation also works for adding new properties: settings["maxWidth"] = 1200.

practice.task: Create an object called config with properties host: "localhost" and port: 3000. Use a variable to access the port, then use bracket notation to add a property called max-retries (with a hyphen).
hints: Store the key in a variable: let key = "port"; then config[key].
Dot notation can't handle the hyphen — that's why bracket notation exists.
practice.note: Use dot notation by default — switch to bracket notation only when you need dynamic keys or keys with special characters.

keyTakeaways: Dot notation (obj.key) is clean and preferred for known property names.
Bracket notation (obj["key"]) is required for dynamic keys, variables, or keys with spaces.
Bracket notation also works for adding new properties to an object.
lessons.challenge: Given let data = {"user-name": "Alex", "user-age": 25}, write a function that takes a string like "user-name" and returns the corresponding value using bracket notation.

lessons.title: Object Destructuring & Property Shorthands
lessons.description: Extract values from objects in one line — destructuring makes code shorter and more readable.

sections.heading: What is destructuring?
paragraphs: Destructuring lets you pull values out of an object and assign them to variables in a single statement. Instead of writing obj.name repeatedly, you extract name once and use it directly.
list: Syntax: const { name, age } = obj;
Creates variables matching the property names
You can rename variables: const { name: userName } = obj;
You can set default values: const { name = "Unknown" } = obj;

sections.heading: Shorthand property syntax
paragraphs: When creating an object, if the variable name matches the property name, you can skip the colon and value — just use the variable name.
list: Instead of { name: name }, write { name }
Instead of { age: age, role: role }, write { age, role }
This only works when variable and property names are the same

codeExamples.heading: Basic destructuring
explanation: const { name, age } = user; creates two variables with values from the object.
Renaming uses a colon after the key: name: userName means "take user.name and put it in userName".
The original object is not modified — destructuring only reads values.
codeExamples.output:
> console.log(name);  // "Alex"
> console.log(age);   // 25
> console.log(userName);  // "Alex"
> console.log(location);  // "New York"
"Alex"
25
"Alex"
"New York"

codeExamples.heading: Shorthand properties and defaults
explanation: Shorthand: { name, age, role } is the same as { name: name, age: age, role: role }.
Defaults: port = 3000 means if port is missing, use 3000.
Defaults only kick in for undefined values — they won't override null.

practice.task: Given let settings = { theme: "dark", fontSize: 14, language: "en" }, use destructuring to extract all three properties. Then create a new object using shorthand syntax from three variables.
hints: This is how React components commonly pass props.
practice.note: Destructuring with const prevents accidental reassignment of extracted values.

keyTakeaways: Destructuring extracts object properties into variables: const { name, age } = obj;.
You can rename extracted variables and set default values.
Shorthand property syntax { name, age } replaces { name: name, age: age }.
lessons.challenge: Write a function greet({ name, age, city = "Unknown" }) that uses parameter destructuring to log a greeting like "Hello Alex from New York, you are 25!".

lessons.title: Object Utilities: Object.keys(), Object.values(), Object.entries()
lessons.description: Three built-in methods that convert objects into arrays — making them easy to loop, filter, and transform.

sections.heading: Why convert objects to arrays?
paragraphs: Objects aren't arrays — you can't use forEach, map, or filter directly on them. But Object.keys(), Object.values(), and Object.entries() convert objects into arrays so you can use all array methods.
list: Object.keys(obj) — returns an array of all property names (keys)
Object.values(obj) — returns an array of all property values
Object.entries(obj) — returns an array of [key, value] pairs

sections.heading: Working with the results
paragraphs: These methods return arrays, so you can chain array methods like map, filter, and forEach on them. This is the standard way to iterate over object properties in modern JavaScript.
list: Use .map() to transform keys or values
Use .filter() to keep specific entries
Use .forEach() to loop through entries

codeExamples.heading: Object.keys, values, entries
explanation: Object.keys() gives you the property names as an array.
Object.values() gives you the property values as an array.
Object.entries() gives you [key, value] pairs — useful when you need both.

codeExamples.heading: Iterating with entries
explanation: Object.entries(scores) creates an array of [subject, score] pairs.
Destructuring in forEach: ([subject, score]) unpacks each pair.
.filter() works on the array, keeping only pairs where score > 90.

practice.task: Given let prices = { apple: 1.5, banana: 0.75, orange: 1.25 }, use Object.entries and forEach to log each fruit and price. Then use filter to find items under $1.
hints: Remember: entries gives you [key, value] arrays — destructure them!
practice.note: Object.keys and Object.values are simpler when you only need one half of the data.

keyTakeaways: Object.keys() returns property names, Object.values() returns values, Object.entries() returns [key, value] pairs.
All three return arrays, so you can use map, filter, and forEach on them.
These are the standard ways to iterate over object properties in modern JavaScript.
lessons.challenge: Given let inventory = { shirts: 10, pants: 5, shoes: 0, hats: 3 }, use Object.entries to find all items with zero stock. Then use Object.keys to get a list of in-stock items.

lessons.title: Parsing & Stringifying JSON Data (JSON.parse, JSON.stringify)
lessons.description: JSON is the universal format for exchanging data between servers and browsers — learn to convert between JSON strings and JavaScript objects.

sections.heading: What is JSON?
paragraphs: JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) is a text format that looks like a JavaScript object but is just a string. APIs send data as JSON strings, and you need to convert them to objects to use them in your code.
list: JSON only supports strings, numbers, booleans, null, arrays, and objects
Keys must be double-quoted strings: {"name": "Alex"}
No functions, no undefined, no comments in JSON

sections.heading: Converting between JSON and objects
list: JSON.parse(jsonString) — converts a JSON string into a JavaScript object
JSON.stringify(object) — converts a JavaScript object into a JSON string
Parse to use data; stringify to send or store data

codeExamples.heading: JSON.parse and JSON.stringify
explanation: JSON.parse() turns the string into a real object you can use with dot notation.
JSON.stringify() turns an object into a string — useful for sending to a server or saving.
The stringified version has no spaces between properties by default.

codeExamples.heading: Pretty-printing and nested objects
explanation: Adding null, 2 as arguments to stringify formats the output with 2-space indentation.
JSON handles nested objects and arrays perfectly.
You can round-trip data: stringify then parse to get a deep copy.

practice.task: Create an object with at least 3 properties. Stringify it, then parse it back. Verify the result matches the original using console.log.
hints: Start with let original = { name: "Test", items: [1, 2, 3], active: true };
practice.note: JSON.stringify can't handle functions, undefined, or symbols — they get dropped or converted.

keyTakeaways: JSON.parse() converts a JSON string into a JavaScript object.
JSON.stringify() converts a JavaScript object into a JSON string.
JSON is the standard format for sending data to/from servers and APIs.
lessons.challenge: Write a function that takes a JavaScript object, deep clones it using JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(obj)), and returns the clone. Test with a nested object to confirm it's a true copy.

lessons.title: Working with Web URLs via URL & URLSearchParams APIs
lessons.description: The built-in URL API makes parsing and building URLs easy — no more manual string splitting.

sections.heading: Why use the URL API?
paragraphs: URLs are strings, but manually parsing them with string methods is error-prone. The built-in URL and URLSearchParams APIs give you a clean, structured way to work with URLs — extracting parts, modifying parameters, and building new URLs.
list: new URL(string) — parses a URL string into parts
URLSearchParams — reads and modifies query parameters
Works in browsers and Node.js 10+

sections.heading: URL object properties
list: .href — the full URL string
.origin — protocol + hostname + port
.pathname — the path after the domain
.search — the query string including ?
.hash — the fragment including #
.hostname — the domain name

codeExamples.heading: Parsing a URL
codeExamples.code:
let url = new URL("https://example.com:8080/products?color=red&size=large#reviews");

console.log(url.hostname);  // "example.com"
console.log(url.port);      // "8080"
console.log(url.pathname);  // "/products"
console.log(url.search);    // "?color=red&size=large"
console.log(url.hash);      // "#reviews"
console.log(url.origin);    // "https://example.com:8080"
explanation: new URL() automatically parses the string into structured parts.
Each part is accessible as a property — no manual string splitting needed.
This works with any valid URL, even complex ones with ports and fragments.
codeExamples.output:
> console.log(url.hostname);  // "example.com"
> console.log(url.port);      // "8080"
> console.log(url.pathname);  // "/products"
> console.log(url.search);    // "?color=red&size=large"
> console.log(url.hash);      // "#reviews"
> console.log(url.origin);    // "https://example.com:8080"
"example.com"
"8080"
"/products"
"?color=red&size=large"
"#reviews"
"https://example.com:8080"

codeExamples.heading: Working with query parameters
explanation: url.searchParams gives you a URLSearchParams object for easy access.
.get() reads a single parameter; .set() adds or updates one.
Changes to searchParams automatically update the URL string (.href).
codeExamples.output:
> console.log(params.get("q"));       // "javascript"
> console.log(params.get("page"));    // "2"
> console.log(url.href);
> console.log(url.href);
> console.log(params.has("q"));  // true
"javascript"
"2"
true

practice.task: Create a URL object from "https://api.example.com/users?page=1&limit=10". Extract the pathname, then add a new parameter sort=name and log the updated URL.
practice.note: URLSearchParams also supports .append(), .keys(), .values(), and .forEach() for iteration.

keyTakeaways: new URL() parses a URL string into a structured object with hostname, pathname, search, and more.
url.searchParams provides methods to get, set, delete, and check query parameters.
Changes to searchParams automatically update the URL — no manual string building required.
lessons.challenge: Write a function buildUrl(base, params) that takes a base URL string and an object of parameters, and returns the full URL with all parameters added using the URL API.
